medications.name: IKACOR / IKAKOR — verapamil
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data document 5-mg ampoules and 40-mg tablets.
medications.administration: IV verapamil is given slowly over at least 2 minutes under continuous ECG and BP monitoring; oral verapamil is a separate formulation.
medications.use: Selected supraventricular arrhythmias/rate control and antianginal therapy.
medications.monitor: • Watch HR, rhythm and BP. • Report bradycardia, AV block or significant hypotension. • Constipation is common with oral therapy. • Be very cautious when IV verapamil overlaps with beta-blockade.
medications.why: Verapamil slows AV-node conduction and myocardial activity; combining AV-node blockers can cause excessive depression.

medications.memoryDanger: Bradycardia, AV block and hypotension; beta-blocker overlap can be dangerous.

medications.name: ENALAPRIL
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data document 5- and 20-mg tablets.
medications.administration: PO. Check current BP and whether the patient is volume-depleted before administration.
medications.use: Chronic cardiovascular therapy for selected hypertension and heart-failure patients.
medications.monitor: • Monitor BP. • Follow potassium and renal function when ordered. • New lip/tongue/face swelling requires urgent escalation. • Previous ACE-inhibitor angioedema is a contraindication.
medications.why: ACE inhibition lowers angiotensin II/aldosterone, which lowers BP but can raise potassium and alter kidney function.

medications.memoryUse: ACE inhibitor for selected HTN/HF patients.
medications.memoryDanger: Angioedema is an airway emergency; also monitor K+ and renal function.

medications.name: TROVAN / LIPIDEX / LIPDIX — atorvastatin
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian data support 20- and 40-mg atorvastatin options; TROVAN 40 mg is registry-confirmed.
medications.administration: PO; no special bedside preparation.
medications.use: Secondary cardiovascular prevention, including after ACS.
medications.monitor: • Mild muscle symptoms can occur. • Severe unexplained muscle pain/weakness ± dark urine is a rare red flag for myopathy/rhabdomyolysis. • Do not make rare rhabdomyolysis sound routine. • Flag major new interacting medicines rather than memorizing an exhaustive list.
medications.why: Its main CCU role is long-term cardiovascular risk reduction, not acute chest-pain relief.

medications.name: LASIX — furosemide
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data document a 20-mg ampoule, 40-mg tablet and a higher-strength injectable presentation.
medications.administration: PO or slow IV. Routine IV doses are given slowly; the source reference notes high-dose parenteral therapy should use controlled infusion and avoid rates faster than about 4 mg/min. Verify the actual product/order.
medications.use: Pulmonary/peripheral congestion and fluid overload, including selected acute heart-failure patients.
medications.monitor: • Track urine output and congestion. • Check BP. • Follow K+, Mg2+, Na+ and renal function. • Report tinnitus/hearing change, especially with large/rapid IV doses. • Routine oral doses are often given earlier in the day to reduce nocturia.
medications.why: Loop diuresis removes sodium/water rapidly but can deplete electrolytes and volume.

medications.memoryUse: Strong loop diuretic for fluid overload/pulmonary congestion.
medications.memoryDanger: Hypotension, electrolyte loss and high/rapid-dose ototoxicity.
medications.mechanism: Blocks the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending loop of Henle.

medications.name: FARIGM — dapagliflozin
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data document 10-mg tablets.
medications.administration: PO only; it has no acute glucose-correction role.
medications.use: Chronic therapy for diabetes, heart failure and kidney disease depending on the patient.
medications.monitor: • Watch volume status/BP. • Ask about genital or urinary symptoms. • In acutely ill, fasting or NPO patients, verify whether the drug is intentionally held. • Remember euglycemic ketoacidosis can occur without very high glucose.
medications.why: SGLT2 blockade increases urinary glucose/sodium loss; this helps chronic disease but can contribute to dehydration and ketoacidosis risk.

medications.memoryDanger: Acute illness/NPO + euglycemic DKA is the key CCU red flag.

medications.name: SLIDING-SCALE / CORRECTION INSULIN
medications.drugclass: High-alert insulin therapy; usually regular human insulin or a rapid-acting analogue for correction.
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data include regular U-100 vials and rapid-acting U-100 pens among other insulin formulations.
medications.administration: Correction insulin is normally SC using the ordered glucose-correction scale. IV insulin is a different protocol and requires a dedicated pump; never assume 'sliding scale' means IV.
medications.use: Correction of hyperglycemia according to the current order/protocol.
medications.monitor: • Check current bedside glucose. • Verify exact insulin name, concentration, dose and meal/NPO status. • Recheck glucose per protocol. • Hypoglycemia is the immediate major hazard. • Follow product-specific storage limits.
medications.why: Insulin is high-alert because type, concentration and timing errors can cause severe hypoglycemia.

medications.memoryDanger: Wrong insulin/type/dose/timing can cause severe hypoglycemia.

medications.name: NOREPINEPHRINE / NORADRENALINE
medications.drugclass: Catecholamine vasopressor; predominantly alpha1 with beta1 activity.
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data document 4-mg ampoules.
medications.administration: Dilute to the hospital-standard concentration and run as a continuous infusion on an infusion pump; never IV push. Central access is preferred for ongoing/concentrated therapy, but a suitable proximal peripheral line may be used short-term when urgent therapy should not be delayed.
medications.use: Vasopressor support for severe hypotension/shock when clinically indicated.
medications.monitor: • Continuous/very frequent BP and perfusion assessment. • Inspect any peripheral IV frequently. • Pain, pallor, swelling, coolness or loss of flow at the site requires immediate action/escalation. • Pump precision matters because small rate changes can materially change BP.
medications.why: Strong vasoconstriction raises systemic vascular resistance/MAP; extravasation can cause local ischemia.

medications.name: DOBUTAMINE
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data document 250-mg ampoules.
medications.administration: The concentrate must be diluted and given by continuous infusion pump; never IV push. Use the local standardized concentration rather than memorizing one bag volume.
medications.use: Selected low-cardiac-output states such as severe acute HF/cardiogenic shock when increased contractility is needed.
medications.monitor: • Continuous ECG/HR and BP. • Follow urine output and peripheral perfusion. • Watch for tachycardia, ectopy and BP changes. • Peripheral administration may be used with close site monitoring; central access is preferable for concentrated/prolonged therapy.
medications.why: Dobutamine increases cardiac contractility/output — think PUMP — but can provoke tachyarrhythmia.

medications.name: DOPAMINE
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data document 200-mg ampoules.

medications.monitor: • Continuous HR/rhythm/BP. • Check urine output/peripheral perfusion. • Watch for tachyarrhythmia, excessive vasoconstriction and extravasation. • A large peripheral vein may be used initially with frequent inspection; central access is preferred for prolonged/concentrated infusion.
medications.why: Effects change with dose; excessive exposure can become pro-arrhythmic or strongly vasoconstrictive.

medications.name: ATROPINE
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data document 1-mg ampoules.
medications.administration: For symptomatic bradycardia, given as an IV/IO bolus according to the current resuscitation protocol; not normally a continuous infusion.

medications.name: PANTOVER / PANTOVERE — pantoprazole

medications.name: VENTOLIN — salbutamol / albuterol
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data document nebulizer solution and 100-mcg/inhalation aerosol; Palestinian product records also document Ventolin forms.
medications.administration: Inhaled by inhaler or nebulizer. For nebulization, measure the ordered dose and dilute with 0.9% NaCl only when required by the device/order. It is not a routine IV medication.
medications.use: Relief of bronchospasm/wheeze in the appropriate respiratory patient.
medications.monitor: • Reassess work of breathing, wheeze and SpO2. • Monitor HR and tremor. • Repeated/high nebulized doses can lower K+. • Low potassium matters more when the patient is also receiving furosemide or already has hypokalemia.

medications.name: NYSTATIN
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian medicine data include an oral nystatin preparation; a common suspension strength is 100,000 units/mL.
medications.administration: Shake well, measure accurately, distribute around the mouth and retain as long as practical before swallowing. Avoid immediate food/drink when possible.
medications.use: Commonly used for oral candidiasis.
medications.monitor: • Inspect oral lesions and response. • Nausea, GI upset or oral irritation can occur. • Oral nystatin is not a treatment for systemic fungal infection. • Follow the local product storage label.
medications.why: Oral nystatin acts locally and is minimally absorbed.

medications.name: MEDIUM — betahistine
medications.availability: YES for betahistine 16-mg tablets. 'Medium' is the ward-reported trade spelling and should be verified against the package.
medications.administration: PO; taking it with or after food may reduce stomach upset.

medications.monitor: • Common effects include nausea, dyspepsia and headache. • Use more caution with asthma or peptic-ulcer history. • Verify the package says betahistine because the trade spelling is ward-reported.
medications.why: Lower-priority symptom-control medicine in CCU compared with acute cardiac drugs.

medications.name: PROFEX — propafenone
medications.availability: WARD-REPORTED in your CCU for the exact trade product. Current manufacturer information supports PROFEX 150-mg and 300-mg oral tablets; this update did not locate a current Palestinian public registry entry for that exact brand.
medications.administration: PO tablets. Verify exact strength/schedule from the package and Kardex. This is not an IV emergency-trolley formulation; rhythm-control strategy is cardiology-directed.
medications.use: Rhythm control in carefully selected patients with arrhythmias such as AF/flutter, PSVT and some ventricular arrhythmias; not appropriate for every AF patient.
medications.monitor: • Check HR, BP and ECG/rhythm when clinically indicated. • Hold/escalate for marked bradycardia, hypotension, new/worsening arrhythmia, important conduction slowing or QRS widening. • Structural heart disease, recent MI, HF or conduction disease can make Class Ic therapy unsafe. • Review electrolytes and other conduction-slowing drugs. • Some beta-blocking activity means bronchospasm risk matters.
medications.why: Fast sodium-channel blockade slows conduction; that can suppress arrhythmia but can also create dangerous conduction/proarrhythmic effects.
medications.source: Routine CCU meds · approved bedside format Sep 2026
medications.memoryUse: Class Ic rhythm-control antiarrhythmic.
medications.memoryDanger: Structural heart disease/recent MI/HF and conduction problems are important safety issues.
medications.mechanism: Blocks fast cardiac sodium channels and slows conduction.

medications.name: VALZADEPINE / 'Valzadipine' — amlodipine + valsartan
medications.drugclass: Combination antihypertensive: dihydropyridine CCB + angiotensin-II receptor blocker (ARB).
medications.availability: YES. Valzadepine is a Palestinian Pharmacare product; Palestinian-market evidence supports amlodipine/valsartan combinations such as 5/80, 5/160 and 10/160 mg. Verify the exact strength on the package.
medications.administration: PO tablet. No IV preparation/pump. Give the exact ordered combination strength; do not mentally split the components unless separate products are actually ordered.
medications.use: Chronic hypertension treatment when one drug alone is insufficient.
medications.monitor: • Check BP and dizziness/hypotension. • Monitor renal function and potassium as ordered because valsartan can affect kidney function and raise K+. • Look for ankle edema from amlodipine. • Avoid in pregnancy. • Do not confuse it with valsartan + hydrochlorothiazide.
medications.why: Amlodipine relaxes arteries while valsartan blocks angiotensin-II effects.
medications.source: Routine CCU meds · approved bedside format Sep 2026
medications.memoryUse: Amlodipine + valsartan combination for hypertension.
medications.memoryDanger: Do not confuse with valsartan/HCTZ; monitor BP, renal function and K+.
medications.mechanism: Combines arterial calcium-channel blockade with angiotensin-II receptor blockade.
medications.mechanismBasis: Source-derived from the approved CCU medication references in this project; exact product/container instructions and current local protocol still take priority.

medications.name: VALZAN HCT — valsartan + hydrochlorothiazide
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian MoH data list VALZAN-HCT as a local Pharmacare product; Palestinian product data document multiple valsartan/HCTZ strengths.
medications.administration: PO film-coated tablet. Give the exact ordered strength; do not assume one combination strength is interchangeable with another.
medications.use: Hypertension when monotherapy is insufficient. You observed this combination being used in CCU instead of Valzadepine in some patients; that is a treatment choice, not a dose-for-dose substitution.
medications.monitor: • Check BP and orthostatic symptoms. • Follow renal function and electrolytes, especially Na+ and K+. • HCTZ can lower Na+/K+ and cause volume depletion while valsartan can raise K+, so do not guess the net K+ effect. • Watch hydration/volume status. • Avoid in pregnancy. • Do not confuse with Valzadepine.
medications.why: Valsartan blocks angiotensin II while HCTZ increases sodium/water excretion.

medications.memoryUse: Valsartan + HCTZ combination for hypertension.
medications.memoryDanger: Electrolyte/volume changes plus ARB renal/K+ effects require monitoring.
medications.mechanism: Combines angiotensin-II receptor blockade with thiazide diuresis.

medications.name: SYMBICORT — budesonide + formoterol
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian MoH registry lists SYMBICORT TURBUHALER 160/4.5 mcg per inhalation in 60- and 120-dose inhalers.
medications.administration: Inhaled dry-powder Turbuhaler. Inhale forcefully/deeply through the mouthpiece and do not exhale into it. Rinse the mouth after maintenance doses. Use the exact prescribed regimen.
medications.use: Ongoing asthma or COPD treatment in a CCU patient with chronic respiratory disease; not an IV or nebulized CCU drug.
medications.monitor: • Check inhaler technique. • Rinse mouth to reduce thrush/hoarseness. • Monitor tremor, palpitations or tachycardia from formoterol, especially in cardiac patients. • Rare red flag: immediate worsening bronchospasm after inhalation. • Increasing reliever need or worsening symptoms requires reassessment.
medications.why: Budesonide reduces airway inflammation; formoterol bronchodilates.

medications.memoryUse: Maintenance inhaler combining anti-inflammatory steroid + long-acting bronchodilator.
medications.memoryDanger: Poor technique reduces effect; rinse mouth; monitor cardiac beta2 effects.
medications.mechanism: ICS reduces airway inflammation; LABA stimulates beta2 receptors.

medications.name: GENTAMICIN
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data list gentamicin 80-mg injection; Palestinian registry data also support an 80 mg/2 mL product.
medications.administration: IV infusion or IM depending on the order/product. The referenced 80 mg/2 mL product is diluted for IV use; intermittent IV administration is infused over the product-specified period. Follow the exact local product/protocol.
medications.use: Treatment of serious susceptible bacterial infections, especially Gram-negative infection, when selected by the treating team.
medications.monitor: • Check renal function before/during therapy. • Dosing often requires renal adjustment; do not alter it independently. • Monitor serum levels when ordered/available. • Watch for ototoxicity: tinnitus, hearing change, dizziness/vertigo. • Watch for nephrotoxicity: rising creatinine/falling urine output. • Do not casually premix with other drugs without confirmed compatibility.
medications.why: Gentamicin is renally cleared and has a narrow safety margin; accumulation can injure kidneys and the vestibular/auditory system.

medications.memoryUse: Aminoglycoside for serious susceptible infections.
medications.memoryDanger: Nephrotoxicity + ototoxicity; renal function and levels matter.
medications.mechanism: Binds the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit and disrupts protein synthesis.

medications.name: AEROVENT — ipratropium bromide
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian MoH drug-price data list AEROVENT SOLUTION as ipratropium bromide. Verify the exact ward bottle/concentration.
medications.administration: Nebulized/inhaled solution; not IV. Give the exact ordered dose using the nebulizer/device. It may be combined with salbutamol when ordered. Do not assume one dilution volume across products.
medications.use: Bronchodilation in bronchospasm, especially COPD and some asthma exacerbations.
medications.monitor: • Reassess work of breathing, wheeze, RR and SpO2. • Dry mouth/throat irritation can occur. • Avoid directing nebulized mist into the eyes. • Use caution in patients prone to urinary retention. • Worsening respiratory distress requires reassessment/escalation, not reliance on the nebulizer alone.
medications.why: Ipratropium blocks muscarinic vagal bronchoconstriction, relaxing airway smooth muscle.

medications.memoryUse: SAMA bronchodilator often nebulized for bronchospasm.
medications.memoryDanger: Eye exposure/urinary retention matter; reassess worsening distress.
medications.mechanism: Blocks muscarinic receptors in the airways.

medications.name: ADENOSINE
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data document adenosine 6-mg ampoules.
medications.administration: Rapid IV push followed immediately by a rapid saline flush with continuous ECG monitoring. Use a port as close to the patient as practical. The source reference uses the current AHA adult sequence of 6 mg rapid IV, then 12 mg if required. Do not give it slowly through long tubing.
medications.use: Stable regular narrow-complex SVT; may also be considered in selected stable regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia. Unstable tachyarrhythmia requires the instability pathway/synchronized cardioversion rather than delaying definitive treatment.
medications.monitor: • Continuous ECG/rhythm monitoring. • Warn conscious patients about brief flushing, chest pressure, breathlessness or a frightening pause sensation. • Be prepared for transient AV block/very brief asystole. • Bronchospasm/asthma is an important safety concern. • Theophylline/aminophylline can reduce effect; dipyridamole can increase it.
medications.why: Adenosine is cleared within seconds; rapid push + immediate flush gets enough drug to the AV node before it is metabolized.
medications.source: CCU emergency trolley meds · Deep Research Sep 2026
medications.memoryUse: Rapid AV-node blocker for stable regular SVT.
medications.memoryDanger: Technique is critical; monitor ECG and be ready for transient AV block/asystole.
medications.mechanism: Activates adenosine A1 receptors in the AV node, causing transient conduction block.

medications.name: LABETALOL
medications.drugclass: Combined alpha1- and beta-adrenergic blocker; antihypertensive.
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine records include a 100-mg injection ampoule and 100-/200-mg tablets. Verify actual ward concentration.
medications.administration: PO or IV. For the verified 5 mg/mL injection, labeling describes slow IV administration over about 2 minutes with BP reassessment; continuous infusion requires a controlled device. Do not copy one schedule to a different product without checking the label.
medications.use: Controlled BP lowering for selected severe hypertension and other physician-directed cardiovascular indications.
medications.monitor: • Check BP, HR and rhythm before/after IV doses. • Hold/clarify for severe bradycardia, important AV block, cardiogenic shock or overt HF. • Bronchial asthma is a contraindication for the referenced injectable formulation because beta2 blockade can provoke bronchospasm. • Check other BP-lowering/AV-node-slowing drugs for additive effects.
medications.why: Alpha1 blockade dilates vessels while beta blockade reduces adrenergic cardiac effects; both BP and HR matter.
medications.source: CCU emergency trolley meds · Deep Research Sep 2026
medications.memoryUse: IV/PO antihypertensive useful when controlled BP reduction is needed.
medications.memoryDanger: Bradycardia, hypotension, AV block and bronchospasm risk.
medications.mechanism: Blocks alpha1 plus beta1/beta2 adrenergic receptors.
medications.mechanismBasis: Source-derived from the approved CCU medication references in this project; exact product/container instructions and current local protocol still take priority.

medications.name: KETAMINE — ketamine hydrochloride
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data document ketamine HCl injection. Vial content is not a universal concentration; read the actual label.
medications.administration: IV or IM according to the prescribed indication. Official labeling for IV anesthetic induction specifies slow administration, about 60 seconds; rapid administration can cause respiratory depression and an excessive pressor response. Sedation/anesthesia requires trained staff, full monitoring and immediately available airway/ventilation equipment.
medications.use: Physician-directed procedural sedation or anesthetic induction when indicated.
medications.monitor: • Check BP, HR, SpO2, breathing and consciousness; ECG as appropriate. • Have suction, oxygen, BVM and resuscitation support ready. • Airway obstruction, laryngospasm or apnea can occur. • BP/HR often rise, but hypotension/cardiac decompensation can also occur. • Emergence reactions can cause confusion/agitation. • Opioid/benzodiazepine combinations increase respiratory-depression risk.
medications.why: NMDA blockade causes dissociative anesthesia; airway and hemodynamic monitoring remain essential.
medications.source: Routine CCU meds · approved bedside format Sep 2026
medications.memoryUse: Dissociative anesthetic/sedative used under monitored, physician-directed conditions.
medications.memoryDanger: Airway/ventilation and hemodynamic monitoring are mandatory.
medications.mechanism: Noncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonism produces dissociative anesthesia.

medications.name: PETHIDINE — meperidine
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data list pethidine injection in 50- and 100-mg ampoules; verify concentration and route.
medications.administration: IM, SC or IV according to the product/order. If IV use is necessary, give very slowly per product labeling, preferably diluted, with monitoring and naloxone/assisted ventilation immediately available. Do not convert ampoule content into a default patient dose.
medications.use: Physician-prescribed analgesia for selected severe pain situations; not a routine first-choice treatment for every CCU chest-pain patient.
medications.monitor: • Check pain, sedation, RR, SpO2 and BP before/after. • Stop/escalate if breathing or consciousness deteriorates. • Nausea, vomiting, dizziness, sedation and hypotension can occur. • Avoid routine/repeated use with renal impairment because normeperidine can accumulate and increase seizure risk. • Review MAO inhibitors and serotonergic/CNS-depressant medicines. • Follow controlled-drug documentation/waste policy.
medications.why: Opioid respiratory depression is the immediate danger; normeperidine accumulation adds a distinctive seizure risk.
medications.source: Routine CCU meds · approved bedside format Sep 2026
medications.memoryUse: Opioid analgesic; use only for a clear prescribed indication.
medications.memoryDanger: Respiratory depression; renal accumulation of normeperidine can provoke seizures.
medications.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor agonism produces analgesia and respiratory/CNS depression.
medications.mechanismBasis: Source-derived from the approved CCU medication references in this project; exact product/container instructions and current local protocol still take priority.

medications.name: MORPHINE — morphine sulfate / hydrochloride
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data include a 10-mg morphine ampoule; verify salt, concentration, route and ordered dose.
medications.administration: IV or IM as appropriate to the product/order. IV morphine is given slowly and titrated under close monitoring, not as an unmonitored rapid bolus. Keep naloxone and airway support available.
medications.use: Selected severe pain/distress management when prescribed; not automatically indicated for every ACS patient or every case of pulmonary edema.
medications.monitor: • Assess pain, RR, SpO2, consciousness and BP before/after. • Sedation can precede respiratory depression. • Hold/escalate for significant respiratory depression, severe hypotension or reduced consciousness; support airway/ventilation and follow naloxone protocol if toxicity is suspected. • Nausea, vomiting, constipation, pruritus and dizziness can occur. • Opioids + benzodiazepines/other sedatives can cause profound respiratory depression. • Follow controlled-drug procedures.
medications.why: Mu-opioid activation relieves severe pain but also reduces respiratory drive and can lower BP.
medications.source: Routine CCU meds · approved bedside format Sep 2026
medications.memoryUse: Strong opioid for selected severe pain/distress when ordered.
medications.memoryDanger: Respiratory depression and hypotension; naloxone/airway support must be available.
medications.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor agonist.
medications.mechanismBasis: Source-derived from the approved CCU medication references in this project; exact product/container instructions and current local protocol still take priority.

medications.name: SPIRONOLACTONE — Aldactone
medications.availability: YES. Palestine-wide records show spironolactone 25- and 100-mg tablets; exact brand may differ.
medications.administration: PO tablets. No routine IV emergency formulation, reconstitution, IV line or pump.
medications.use: Mainly chronic/subacute therapy in HFrEF, resistant hypertension and aldosterone-mediated fluid retention; not the rapid-diuresis rescue role of IV furosemide.
medications.monitor: • Check potassium and renal function. • Escalate significant hyperkalemia or worsening renal function before routine administration. • Watch hypotension, dizziness and dehydration with other diuretics/RAAS blockers. • Do not casually add potassium supplements or potassium-containing salt substitutes.
medications.why: Spironolactone saves potassium and blocks aldosterone; furosemide provides stronger, faster diuresis and tends to waste potassium.
medications.source: CCU emergency trolley meds · Deep Research Sep 2026
medications.memoryUse: Aldosterone-blocking, potassium-sparing diuretic; especially useful in HFrEF/aldosterone-driven states.
medications.memoryDanger: Hyperkalemia is the key danger, especially with renal impairment.
medications.mechanism: Blocks mineralocorticoid receptors, reducing aldosterone-mediated sodium retention and potassium loss.

medications.name: LIDOCAINE HCl
medications.drugclass: Class IB ventricular antiarrhythmic; also a local anesthetic.
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data document lidocaine HCl injection in 1%, 2% and 4% presentations.
medications.administration: Before IV cardiac use, verify the product is intended for IV antiarrhythmic use and contains no epinephrine/local-anesthetic additive. For perfusing ventricular arrhythmias, the source reference uses controlled IV dosing/infusion; cardiac-arrest use follows the current AHA algorithm.
medications.use: AHA allows lidocaine or amiodarone for shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT; it may also be used for selected ventricular arrhythmias with a pulse.
medications.monitor: • Continuous ECG during IV antiarrhythmic use. • Worsening conduction, QRS widening, bradycardia or new arrhythmia needs immediate reassessment. • Watch neurologic toxicity: perioral numbness, confusion, drowsiness, tinnitus, twitching or seizures. • Hypotension, myocardial depression, heart block and respiratory depression can occur with excessive exposure.
medications.why: Cardiac sodium-channel blockade suppresses ventricular arrhythmia, while systemic toxicity often appears as neurologic or conduction changes.
medications.source: CCU emergency trolley meds · Deep Research Sep 2026
medications.memoryUse: Ventricular antiarrhythmic; also a local anesthetic, so verify the formulation.
medications.memoryDanger: Neurologic toxicity and conduction depression; local-anesthetic products with additives are not automatically suitable for IV cardiac use.

medications.name: SODIUM BICARBONATE
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian MoH essential-medicine data document sodium bicarbonate 8.4% injection; container volume can vary.
medications.administration: IV. The adult 8.4% emergency formulation is highly concentrated. Do not convert percentage, mL and mEq from memory; administration/dilution depend on the indication and actual product/protocol.
medications.use: Not routine in undifferentiated cardiac arrest. Use mainly for selected reversible causes/special circumstances such as specific toxicologic/metabolic indications.
medications.monitor: • Verify indication, concentration and ordered mEq. • Follow sodium, pH/ABG or VBG and potassium when indicated. • Excess can cause alkalemia, hypernatremia and sodium/volume load. • Do not improvise Y-site mixing with emergency drugs unless compatibility is confirmed. • It never substitutes for high-quality CPR/defibrillation/ventilation or treatment of the cause.
medications.why: It changes acid-base chemistry; without a specific indication it can add sodium/alkali without fixing the cause.

medications.memoryUse: Special-circumstance alkalinizing therapy; not a routine arrest drug.
medications.memoryDanger: Concentration/mEq errors, alkalemia and sodium load; verify the indication.

medications.name: HYDRALAZINE
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data document 20-mg ampoules and 50-mg tablets.
medications.administration: Parenteral products may be IV or IM. Because push instructions vary across products, give slow IV only according to the exact ampoule insert/local protocol rather than memorizing an invented universal rate.
medications.use: Parenteral treatment of severe hypertension when indicated.
medications.monitor: • Check BP before and repeatedly after parenteral administration. • Watch headache, flushing, dizziness, hypotension and reflex tachycardia. • Escalate new chest discomfort or marked tachycardia in a coronary patient. • Do not confuse with labetalol: hydralazine can increase reflex HR.
medications.why: Direct arteriolar dilation can drop BP and trigger reflex sympathetic tachycardia.

medications.memoryUse: Direct vasodilator used for selected severe hypertension.
medications.memoryDanger: Reflex tachycardia/hypotension can be clinically important in coronary patients.

medications.name: DEXTROSE 50% — D50
medications.availability: YES for dextrose 50% in Palestinian documentation; a specific 25-g/50-mL Palestinian emergency syringe was not independently confirmed in the source research.
medications.administration: IV only for the concentrated emergency product. Ensure a clearly patent IV, preferably a good large peripheral vein for a single emergency dose, and stop if infiltration/extravasation is suspected. Verify grams and volume on the actual container.
medications.use: Severe symptomatic hypoglycemia when IV glucose is indicated.

medications.why: D50 raises glucose rapidly but is very hypertonic and can injure tissue if it leaves the vein.

medications.memoryUse: Concentrated IV glucose for severe symptomatic hypoglycemia.
medications.memoryDanger: Extravasation can injure tissue; always recheck glucose and consciousness.

medications.name: HYDROCORTISONE
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data document a 100-mg vial.
medications.administration: Product-specific IV injection/infusion or IM administration. Emergency products are commonly hydrocortisone sodium succinate; verify the salt, vial strength and reconstitution from the exact product.
medications.use: Adrenal crisis and selected severe inflammatory/allergic or shock states when indicated. In anaphylaxis it is an adjunct and must not delay epinephrine.

medications.why: Steroids alter inflammatory and stress responses; benefit is diagnosis-specific and not immediate cardiac resuscitation.

medications.name: DIAZEPAM
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian documentation includes 10-mg ampoules and 5-mg tablets; injectable products are available.
medications.administration: IV or IM depending on the product/order. For the referenced injectable formulation, do not mix/dilute in a syringe/infusion container; direct IV administration is slow. Follow the exact product instructions.
medications.use: Seizure/status epilepticus, severe agitation or selected procedural sedation; not a cardiac antiarrhythmic.
medications.monitor: • Have airway support, oxygen and resuscitation capability immediately available. • Monitor RR, SpO2, consciousness and BP. • Opioid + benzodiazepine exposure markedly increases respiratory-depression risk. • Use extra caution in chronic lung disease/frailty/unstable cardiovascular status. • Inspect the IV site because diazepam can irritate veins.

medications.name: AMIODARONE — PROCOR
medications.drugclass: Predominantly Class III antiarrhythmic with multiple channel and adrenergic effects.
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian documentation includes amiodarone HCl 150-mg ampoules and 200-mg tablets; PROCOR 200 mg = amiodarone, not a separate drug.
medications.administration: IV ampoules are concentrated and require the product-specific dilution/infusion setup. The source reference distinguishes perfusing ventricular-arrhythmia infusion from cardiac-arrest dosing; use a pump for controlled infusions and follow exact line/filter instructions.
medications.use: Selected serious ventricular arrhythmias and shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT; exact regimen depends on whether the patient has a pulse and the rhythm/algorithm.
medications.monitor: • Continuous ECG and BP during IV use. • Watch hypotension and bradycardia. • Monitor QT and correct important K+/Mg2+ abnormalities when feasible. • Inspect peripheral IV sites for phlebitis. • Review digoxin because amiodarone can increase digoxin exposure and both slow AV conduction. • Do not confuse the PROCOR tablet with the IV ampoule.
medications.why: Amiodarone changes cardiac conduction/repolarization; arrest and perfusing-arrhythmia regimens differ because the clinical situations differ.

medications.memoryUse: Broad antiarrhythmic used for serious ventricular rhythms and refractory VF/pVT.
medications.memoryDanger: Hypotension/bradycardia/QT effects; arrest dose and perfusing infusion are different.
medications.mechanism: Blocks multiple ion channels and has antiadrenergic effects.

medications.name: CALCIUM GLUCONATE
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian MoH data document calcium gluconate 10% × 10 mL.
medications.administration: Dilution/rate depend on indication and product. Use only manufacturer/hospital directions rather than memorizing a universal push rule. Secure IV access is essential.
medications.use: Severe symptomatic hypocalcemia and myocardial membrane stabilization in severe hyperkalemia with ECG toxicity when indicated. Calcium does not remove potassium from the body.
medications.monitor: • ECG/rhythm monitoring during urgent administration. • Confirm the IV is secure; extravasation can injure tissue. • Check serum calcium/indication when circumstances permit. • Do not casually mix calcium and sodium bicarbonate in the same syringe/line because precipitation can occur. • Calcium gluconate and calcium chloride are not equivalent in elemental calcium.
medications.why: In hyperkalemia, calcium protects the myocardium electrically while other therapies shift or remove potassium.
medications.source: CCU emergency trolley meds · Deep Research Sep 2026
medications.memoryUse: Membrane stabilizer in severe hyperkalemia with ECG toxicity; also treats hypocalcemia.
medications.memoryDanger: Extravasation injury and product-equivalence mistakes; calcium does not lower serum K+.
medications.mechanism: Raises extracellular calcium and stabilizes cardiac membrane excitability.
medications.mechanismBasis: Source-derived from the approved CCU medication references in this project; exact product/container instructions and current local protocol still take priority.

medications.name: MAGNESIUM SULFATE — MgSO4
medications.drugclass: Electrolyte replacement; antiarrhythmic in selected ventricular arrhythmias; anticonvulsant in eclampsia.
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian essential-medicine data document magnesium sulfate injection 50%.
medications.administration: Concentrated magnesium requires controlled administration. Routine IV replacement is diluted/infused rather than given as an uncontrolled rapid push; use the exact product/order for concentration and infusion time.
medications.use: May be considered for recurrent polymorphic VT associated with long-QT syndrome/torsades de pointes; not a generic treatment for every ventricular arrhythmia.
medications.monitor: • Continuous ECG/BP during urgent antiarrhythmic use. • With repeated/high-dose therapy monitor RR, reflexes, urine output/renal function and magnesium level when appropriate. • Toxicity can cause loss of deep-tendon reflexes, hypotension, respiratory depression and conduction abnormalities. • Renal impairment increases accumulation risk. • Calcium salts can antagonize clinically significant magnesium toxicity.
medications.why: Magnesium stabilizes repolarization in torsades; excess magnesium depresses neuromuscular and cardiac conduction.
medications.source: CCU emergency trolley meds · Deep Research Sep 2026
medications.memoryUse: Key electrolyte/antiarrhythmic for torsades with long QT.
medications.memoryDanger: Toxicity = lost reflexes, hypotension, respiratory depression; renal impairment increases risk.
medications.mechanism: Modulates ion transport and membrane stability, including cardiac repolarization.
medications.mechanismBasis: Source-derived from the approved CCU medication references in this project; exact product/container instructions and current local protocol still take priority.

medications.name: DIGOXIN
medications.drugclass: Cardiac glycoside; positive inotrope and AV-nodal slowing agent.
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian documentation includes 0.5-mg ampoules, 0.25-mg tablets and oral liquid.
medications.administration: PO or parenteral depending on the product/order. When IV is used, give slowly rather than as a rapid push; the total loading strategy matters more than treating one ampoule as one standard dose.
medications.use: Option for ventricular rate control in selected AF/flutter patients, but less commonly used for rapid acute rate control because onset is slower. Do not use for pre-excited AF/flutter.
medications.monitor: • Check HR/rhythm before administration. • Review renal function. • Check K+ and Mg2+ when relevant. • Watch nausea/vomiting, confusion, visual disturbance, bradycardia, AV block or new ventricular ectopy as toxicity signals. • Review amiodarone and verapamil interactions. • Interpret a digoxin level with sample timing, renal function and clinical findings.
medications.why: Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic window; kidney function, electrolytes and AV-node interactions strongly change toxicity risk.
medications.source: CCU emergency trolley meds · Deep Research Sep 2026
medications.memoryUse: Cardiac glycoside used for selected rate-control/HF situations.
medications.memoryDanger: Narrow therapeutic window; renal function/electrolytes strongly affect toxicity.
medications.mechanism: Inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase, increasing intracellular calcium and vagal tone.
medications.mechanismBasis: Source-derived from the approved CCU medication references in this project; exact product/container instructions and current local protocol still take priority.

medications.name: AMINOPHYLLINE
medications.availability: YES. Palestinian documentation includes aminophylline 240–250-mg ampoules; exact brand/concentration should be read from the product.
medications.administration: Controlled IV infusion drug, not a casual rapid IV push. Loading/maintenance depend on patient characteristics, recent theophylline/aminophylline exposure and, when available, serum theophylline concentration.
medications.use: Bronchodilator that may still appear on emergency trolleys/local protocols; its narrow therapeutic index and pro-arrhythmic potential are particularly relevant in CCU.
medications.monitor: • Monitor HR/rhythm. • Watch early toxicity: nausea, vomiting, tremor, agitation and persistent tachycardia. • Severe toxicity can progress to seizures and life-threatening arrhythmias. • Check theophylline concentration when clinically available. • Clearance changes with age, illness, smoking and interacting medicines. • Ampoule content is not automatically the patient dose.
medications.why: Aminophylline has a narrow therapeutic range, so extra loading or fast administration can quickly become pro-arrhythmic and neurotoxic.
medications.source: CCU emergency trolley meds · Deep Research Sep 2026
medications.memoryUse: Methylxanthine bronchodilator with a narrow therapeutic range.
medications.memoryDanger: Tachyarrhythmia and seizures are severe toxicity signs.
medications.mechanism: Theophylline-related phosphodiesterase inhibition/adenosine antagonism contributes to bronchodilation and toxicity.

lessons.title: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)

sections.label: Essential meaning
sections.text: ACS = acute myocardial ischemia from reduced coronary blood flow. It includes unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI.

sections.label: Differentiate
sections.text:
• Unstable angina: ischemia without biomarker evidence of myocardial necrosis.
• NSTEMI: myocardial infarction without persistent ST elevation; ECG may show ST depression/T-wave changes.
• STEMI: acute ischemic presentation with compatible ST elevation.

sections.label: Recognize
sections.text:
• Chest pressure/tightness/heaviness
• Radiation to arm, shoulder, jaw, neck, or back
• Dyspnea
• Sweating
• Nausea/vomiting
• Dizziness

sections.label: First nursing actions
sections.text:
• ABC assessment and vital signs
• Cardiac monitoring/rhythm check
• Obtain a 12-lead ECG promptly
• Establish IV access
• Escalate immediately for ischemic ECG changes, hypotension, serious arrhythmia, worsening dyspnea, altered consciousness, or deterioration
• Obtain ordered blood tests and give prescribed ACS treatment
• Oxygen only when indicated by oxygenation/clinical status and local protocol

sections.label: Key rule
sections.text: Do not wait for a biomarker result before escalating a patient with concerning ischemic symptoms, ECG changes, or hemodynamic instability.

lessons.sourceNote: Core Nursing Diagnostic CCU lesson. ACS concepts taught using current ACC/AHA ACS guidance.

lessons.title: Complete Heart Block (CHB)

sections.label: Essential meaning
sections.text: Complete heart block = third-degree AV block. Atrial impulses do not conduct to the ventricles, so atria and ventricles beat independently.

sections.label: ECG hallmark
sections.text: P waves and QRS complexes march separately with no fixed PR relationship. This is AV dissociation.

sections.label: Why it is dangerous
sections.text: A slow ventricular escape rhythm can reduce cardiac output and cause dizziness, syncope, hypotension, confusion, ischemia, acute heart failure, shock, or cardiac arrest.

sections.label: Differentiate from sinus bradycardia
sections.text: Sinus bradycardia: each P wave conducts to a QRS. CHB: P waves and QRS complexes are independent.

sections.label: First nursing actions
sections.text:
• Look at the patient first
• ABC assessment
• Check pulse, BP, consciousness, SpO₂, and symptoms
• Continuous monitoring and 12-lead ECG
• Establish IV access
• Escalate rapidly if symptomatic or unstable
• Prepare for pacing if required

sections.label: Common causes
sections.text:
• MI/ischemia
• Beta-blockers
• Calcium-channel blockers
• Digoxin
• Hypoxia
• Hyperkalemia

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: CHB = atria and ventricles beat independently. If perfusion is poor, escalate and prepare for pacing.

lessons.sourceNote: Core Nursing Diagnostic CCU lesson; bradycardia instability concepts aligned with current AHA guidance.

sections.label: 10 electrodes, 12 leads
sections.text: A 12-lead ECG uses 10 physical electrodes: 4 limb electrodes + 6 chest electrodes. The machine derives 12 electrical views.

sections.label: Electrode vs lead
sections.text: Electrode = the physical sticker/wire touching the patient. Lead = the electrical view the machine sees.

sections.label: Chest electrode placement
sections.text:
• V1: 4th intercostal space, right sternal border
• V2: 4th intercostal space, left sternal border
• V3: halfway between V2 and V4
• V4: 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line
• V5: same horizontal level as V4, anterior axillary line
• V6: same horizontal level as V4, midaxillary line

sections.label: Waves
sections.text: P wave = atrial depolarization. QRS = ventricular depolarization. T wave = ventricular repolarization.

sections.label: Limb colors used locally
sections.text: IEC system commonly seen locally: RA/R = red, LA/L = yellow, LL/F = green, RL/N = black. F = Foot; N = Neutral.

sections.label: Common mistake
sections.text: Placing V1 and V2 too high can create a misleading tracing.

sections.label: What telemetry is
sections.text: Telemetry/bedside ECG monitoring continuously displays cardiac electrical rhythm. It is not the same as a diagnostic 12-lead ECG.

sections.label: 3-lead monitoring
sections.text: A common setup uses three electrodes for continuous heart rate and rhythm monitoring.

sections.label: ECG waveform vs pleth
sections.text: ECG waveform comes from ECG electrodes and reflects electrical activity. Pleth waveform comes from the pulse-oximeter probe and reflects pulsatile blood flow; it gives SpO₂ and pulse rate.

sections.label: Read a rhythm in order
sections.text: Patient → Rate → Regularity → P waves → PR interval → QRS → P/QRS relationship.

sections.label: Useful basics
sections.text:
• 6-second strip: QRS count × 10 ≈ heart rate
• Regular rhythm: 300 ÷ large boxes between R waves
• PR normally about 0.12–0.20 sec
• QRS normally <0.12 sec

sections.label: Artifact rule
sections.text: If the monitor looks chaotic but the patient is awake, talking, and has a strong regular pulse, suspect artifact. Check the patient and pulse before treating the monitor.

lessons.title: Dangerous Rhythms

sections.label: First principle
sections.text: Patient + pulse + rhythm. In suspected arrest, if no definite pulse is found promptly, begin the arrest response.

sections.label: Shockable arrest rhythms
sections.text:
• Ventricular fibrillation (VF)
• Pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT)

sections.label: Non-shockable arrest rhythms
sections.text:
• Pulseless electrical activity (PEA)
• Asystole

sections.label: VT rule
sections.text: Always ask: does the patient have a pulse? Pulseless VT follows the cardiac-arrest pathway. VT with a pulse follows the stable/unstable tachyarrhythmia pathway.

sections.label: PEA
sections.text: PEA means organized electrical activity is seen but there is no pulse. It has no single ECG appearance.

sections.label: Instability signs
sections.text:
• Hypotension
• Acute altered mental status
• Signs of shock
• Ischemic chest discomfort
• Acute heart failure

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: VF + pVT = shockable. PEA + asystole = non-shockable.

lessons.sourceNote: Core Nursing Diagnostic CCU lesson; arrest rhythm classification aligned with current AHA guidance.

lessons.title: Defibrillation vs Cardioversion vs Pacing

sections.label: Start with two questions
sections.text: Does the patient have a pulse? If yes, are they stable or unstable?

sections.label: Defibrillation
sections.text: Unsynchronized shock used for cardiac arrest with VF or pulseless VT. PEA and asystole are not shockable.

sections.label: Synchronized cardioversion
sections.text: A timed shock synchronized to the R wave, typically used for an unstable tachyarrhythmia when a pulse is present.

sections.label: Why synchronization matters
sections.text: Synchronization avoids delivering the shock during the vulnerable T-wave period.

sections.label: Important exception
sections.text: Polymorphic VT requiring shock is treated with an unsynchronized shock because reliable synchronization is not possible.

sections.label: Pacing
sections.text: Repeated electrical stimulation used for dangerous symptomatic bradycardia/high-grade block such as CHB.

sections.label: Capture
sections.text: Electrical capture = pacing spike followed by a QRS. Mechanical capture = a corresponding pulse/BP/perfusion response. Confirm both.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: Defib = VF/pVT arrest. Cardioversion = unstable fast rhythm with pulse. Pacing = dangerous bradycardia.

lessons.sourceNote: Core Nursing Diagnostic CCU lesson; concepts aligned with current AHA guidance.

lessons.title: Sudden Deterioration in CCU: What Do You Do First?

sections.label: Core sequence
sections.text: Patient first → ABC → monitor → identify danger → escalate → reassess.

sections.label: First 30–60 seconds
sections.text:
• A Airway: can the patient talk? Any obstruction?
• B Breathing: RR, effort, SpO₂, breath sounds
• C Circulation: pulse, BP, rhythm, skin/perfusion
• D Disability: consciousness/confusion
• E Exposure: bleeding, edema, lines, obvious cause

sections.label: Red flags
sections.text:
• New severe chest pain
• Sudden dyspnea
• Falling SpO₂
• Hypotension or a marked BP fall
• New confusion/reduced consciousness
• Very fast or very slow heart rate with symptoms
• Dangerous arrhythmia
• Cold/clammy skin or weak pulse
• No pulse
• Sudden major bleeding

sections.label: Practical actions
sections.text:
• ECG + BP + SpO₂ monitoring
• Ensure IV access
• Position appropriately
• Give oxygen when indicated
• Obtain 12-lead ECG when relevant
• Prepare emergency equipment/medications as directed
• Reassess after every intervention

sections.label: Examples
sections.text: Monitor shows VT → look at patient and check pulse. Worsening chest pain → vitals + rhythm + 12-lead + escalate; do not wait for biomarkers. Unresponsive patient → check responsiveness, breathing and pulse; if pulseless, start the arrest response.

sections.label: Essential meaning
sections.text: Cardiogenic shock = the heart cannot pump enough blood to perfuse the organs. Think: weak pump → low cardiac output → organ hypoperfusion.

sections.label: Suspect it when
sections.text:
• Hypotension
• Cold/clammy extremities
• Weak peripheral pulses
• Confusion/reduced consciousness
• Low urine output
• Tachycardia or significant bradycardia
• Dyspnea/crackles may coexist

sections.label: Common CCU causes
sections.text:
• Acute MI
• Severe heart failure
• Serious arrhythmia
• Mechanical complication after MI
• Severe valve dysfunction

sections.label: First nursing response
sections.text: ABC → BP → rhythm → perfusion → escalate. Assess SpO₂/breathing, consciousness, skin, pulses, urine output, and ensure monitoring/IV access.

sections.label: Important mistake
sections.text: Do not automatically give a large IV fluid bolus. If the pump is failing, excess fluid can worsen pulmonary edema.

sections.label: Cardiogenic vs hypovolemic
sections.text: Cardiogenic: pump failure; often cold/clammy, weak pulse, possible crackles/pulmonary edema, JVP may be raised. Hypovolemic: empty tank; often cold/clammy, tachycardic, flat neck veins, clear lungs, with bleeding/dehydration/fluid-loss history.

sections.label: Other shock patterns
sections.text: Distributive shock: vessels are too dilated; septic shock may be warm early. Obstructive shock: flow is blocked, e.g. tension pneumothorax, tamponade, massive PE.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: Cardiogenic = weak pump, often wet lungs/full veins. Hypovolemic = empty tank, usually clear lungs/flat veins. Use the whole clinical picture, not one sign.

lessons.title: Norepinephrine vs Dobutamine

sections.label: The easiest way to remember
sections.text: Norepinephrine = Pressure. Dobutamine = Pump.

sections.label: Norepinephrine
sections.text: Think: the blood pressure/perfusion is too low. Norepinephrine mainly increases vascular tone and raises blood pressure.

sections.label: Dobutamine
sections.text: Think: the heart itself is pumping too weakly. Dobutamine mainly increases cardiac contractility and cardiac output.

sections.label: Why both may be used
sections.text: If a patient has both a weak pump and dangerously low pressure, the team may use dobutamine for pump support and norepinephrine for pressure support.

sections.label: What you monitor
sections.text: Norepinephrine: BP/MAP, rhythm, perfusion, urine output, IV site. Dobutamine: HR/rhythm, BP, perfusion, urine output.

sections.label: Safety memory
sections.text: These are titrated IV infusions. Do not memorize one universal mL/hour rate; the rate depends on the ordered dose and prepared concentration.

lessons.sourceNote: Core Nursing Diagnostic simplified lesson. Drug-specific doses/administration must be checked against the verified medication reference and current local order/protocol.

sections.label: Potassium K⁺
sections.text: Potassium strongly affects cardiac electrical activity. Low K⁺ can cause ectopy/arrhythmias and may show flat T waves or U waves. High K⁺ may show tall peaked T waves and, when severe, widening QRS/bradyarrhythmia/arrest.

sections.label: Magnesium Mg²⁺
sections.text: Low Mg²⁺ makes the heart electrically irritable and can contribute to ventricular arrhythmias. It can also make hypokalemia harder to correct. Magnesium is especially important in torsades de pointes.

sections.label: Calcium Ca²⁺
sections.text: Calcium affects contraction and the QT interval. Low Ca²⁺ tends to prolong QT; high Ca²⁺ tends to shorten QT.

sections.label: Practical CCU example
sections.text: A patient on a loop diuretic develops frequent PVCs. Do not only think 'the rhythm changed'—also check K⁺ and Mg²⁺.

sections.label: Nursing safety
sections.text: If an electrolyte abnormality is accompanied by rhythm/ECG changes, monitor continuously and escalate promptly. Never give IV potassium as a rapid IV push.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: K⁺ = rhythm priority. Mg²⁺ = rhythm stability. Ca²⁺ = contraction + QT.

lessons.title: Furosemide in the CCU

sections.label: Why the patient may receive it
sections.text: Think fluid overload/congestion, especially in heart failure: breathlessness + crackles + edema.

sections.label: What furosemide does
sections.text: Furosemide is a loop diuretic. More urine → less excess fluid → less congestion.

sections.label: What improvement may look like
sections.text:
• Easier breathing
• Less edema
• Fewer crackles
• Reduced fluid overload

sections.label: What the nurse monitors
sections.text:
• BP
• Urine output
• Potassium K⁺
• Renal function
• Overall fluid status

sections.label: Main problems to watch for
sections.text:
• Hypotension
• Excessive volume depletion/dehydration
• Hypokalemia
• Worsening renal function

sections.label: CCU connection
sections.text: If a patient receiving furosemide develops new PVCs or another rhythm change, think about K⁺ and Mg²⁺ as possible contributors.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: Furosemide = remove excess fluid. Watch BP, urine output, kidney function and K⁺.

lessons.sourceNote: Core Nursing Diagnostic CCU lesson. Drug-specific administration remains product/order/protocol specific.

lessons.title: Heart Failure — Practical CCU View

sections.label: Essential meaning
sections.text: Heart failure means the heart cannot pump enough blood effectively or requires abnormally high filling pressures. Clinically, think in two directions: congestion and poor perfusion.

sections.label: Congestion
sections.text: Dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, leg edema, raised JVP, and fluid/weight gain.

sections.label: Poor perfusion
sections.text: Hypotension, cold/clammy skin, weak pulse, confusion, and low urine output.

sections.label: Left vs right
sections.text: Left-sided HF mainly backs up into the lungs → dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, pulmonary edema. Right-sided HF mainly backs up into the systemic veins → peripheral edema, raised JVP, abdominal/hepatic congestion.

sections.label: EF
sections.text: Ejection fraction is the percentage of LV blood ejected with each contraction. HFrEF = reduced EF. HFpEF = preserved EF but impaired filling/stiffness. Do not judge severity from EF alone.

sections.label: Nursing focus
sections.text: Breathing + BP + rhythm + perfusion + urine output + fluid balance. Escalate sudden severe dyspnea, pulmonary edema, falling BP, altered consciousness, dangerous arrhythmia, very low urine output, or ischemic chest pain.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: HF patients may be 'wet' from congestion, 'cold' from poor perfusion, or both.

lessons.sourceNote: Quick clinical reference from this Core Nursing Diagnostic session.

lessons.title: Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM)

sections.label: What it means
sections.text: DCM = dilated cardiomyopathy. The ventricles, especially the LV, become enlarged and contract weakly → cardiac output falls.

sections.label: What it causes
sections.text: Often presents as heart failure: dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, edema, crackles if congested, and arrhythmias. Severe cases can develop low-output states or cardiogenic shock.

sections.label: Common causes
sections.text:
• Genetic/familial disease
• Myocarditis
• Alcohol or cardiotoxic drugs
• Ischemic heart disease/previous MI
• Peripartum cardiomyopathy
• Long-standing tachyarrhythmias
• Some endocrine, metabolic, or nutritional disorders
• Sometimes no clear cause is found

sections.label: Nursing focus
sections.text: Monitor BP, rhythm, SpO₂, breathing, edema, urine output, and perfusion.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: DCM = dilated heart + weak pump → heart failure risk.

lessons.sourceNote: Quick clinical reference from this Core Nursing Diagnostic session.

lessons.title: Ischemic Heart Disease vs Myocardial Infarction

sections.label: IHD
sections.text: Ischemic heart disease is the broader disease state caused by reduced coronary blood supply. It can present as stable angina, unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI, or chronic ischemic cardiomyopathy.

sections.label: MI
sections.text: Myocardial infarction is a specific event in which ischemia is severe/prolonged enough to cause myocardial cell death.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: All MI is ischemic heart disease, but not all ischemic heart disease is MI. A patient with stable exertional angina has IHD but is not necessarily having an MI.

lessons.sourceNote: Quick clinical reference from this Core Nursing Diagnostic session.

lessons.title: Fracture & Limb Safety — Neurovascular Check

sections.label: The one question
sections.text: With any injured or immobilized limb, ask: Is the tissue below the injury still getting enough blood and nerve supply? Check distal to the injury/cast/fixator and compare with the opposite side when possible.

sections.label: Memory sequence
sections.text:
PAIN → BLOOD → FEELING → MOVE → SWELLING.

1) PAIN: Is pain suddenly worsening or much worse than expected?
2) BLOOD: Check color, warmth, capillary refill and distal pulse.
3) FEELING: Ask about numbness, tingling or burning; compare sensation.
4) MOVE: Ask the patient to move distal fingers/toes and compare strength/movement.
5) SWELLING: Look for increasing swelling, a tense limb, or a cast/dressing becoming tight.

sections.label: Compartment syndrome — the emergency
sections.text: Think: pressure building inside the limb. Trauma/fracture → bleeding and swelling → pressure rises inside a closed muscle compartment → tissue perfusion falls → nerves and muscle can be permanently injured.

sections.label: Early warning to remember
sections.text: Severe or increasing pain that is out of proportion to the injury, especially pain made worse by passive stretch, is an important warning. A tense swollen compartment and new paresthesia/weakness add concern. Do not wait for every sign to appear.

sections.label: Critical trap
sections.text: A palpable distal pulse does NOT rule out compartment syndrome. Pallor, paralysis and loss of pulse are late ischemic findings; waiting for the pulse to disappear can delay treatment.

sections.label: What you do
sections.text: If neurovascular status is deteriorating or compartment syndrome is suspected: repeat and document the distal neurovascular check, compare with the opposite limb, check for an obviously constrictive cast/dressing without independently altering prescribed immobilization unless authorized, and escalate urgently to the responsible nurse/orthopaedic team. Continue reassessment. Definitive treatment of confirmed acute compartment syndrome may require urgent fasciotomy.

sections.label: 15-second memory
sections.text: Fracture patient? Check BELOW the injury: PAIN → BLOOD → FEELING → MOVE → SWELLING. Severe increasing pain + pain with passive stretch = compartment-syndrome warning. A pulse does not rule it out.

lessons.sourceNote: IBD2 Nasser orthopaedic lesson. Study baseline: Open RN Health Alterations 10.6 Fracture (distal neurovascular assessment and acute compartment syndrome). Acute-compartment-syndrome warning signs and the importance of serial assessment were checked against the AAOS 2025 Clinical Practice Guideline/resources. Local cast/dressing escalation and intervention must follow the authorized MSF/Nasser IBD2 protocol.

targetedMedications.name: Alteplase (tPA)
targetedMedications.availability: Local Gaza/Palestinian facility stock has not been independently confirmed. Verify the exact product, strength, order, and local protocol.
targetedMedications.use: Emergency thrombolytic used in eligible acute ischemic stroke; current Activase labeling also includes acute myocardial infarction and acute massive pulmonary embolism. Current 2026 AHA/ASA stroke guidance includes alteplase as an IV thrombolytic option for eligible adults within the 4.5-hour treatment window; selected later/unknown-onset cases require advanced-imaging selection.
targetedMedications.administration: IV only and indication-specific. For acute ischemic stroke, current Activase dosing is 0.9 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg), with 10% given as an initial IV bolus and the remainder infused over 60 minutes. MI and massive-PE regimens differ; use the authorized order and current indication-specific protocol. Do not mix other medications into the Activase infusion.
targetedMedications.monitor:
• Major risk: serious bleeding, especially intracranial hemorrhage.
• Before stroke thrombolysis, confirm brain imaging has excluded hemorrhage and verify eligibility/contraindications.
• Monitor BP and neurological status closely; current stroke protocols use BP <185/110 mm Hg before IV thrombolysis and ≤180/105 mm Hg afterward.
• Avoid unnecessary invasive procedures and IM injections; inspect puncture sites and other bleeding sites.
• Sudden severe headache, acute hypertension, nausea/vomiting, or neurological worsening during infusion requires immediate escalation and emergency brain imaging.
• Follow the stroke protocol for post-thrombolysis monitoring and follow-up imaging before antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy.
targetedMedications.why: Alteplase promotes conversion of fibrin-bound plasminogen to plasmin, breaking down fibrin within a thrombus. That can restore blood flow but also creates the major bleeding risk.
targetedMedications.source: Verified update · current DailyMed Activase label + 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline
targetedMedications.pages: DailyMed Activase label (updated Jan 2026); AHA/ASA AIS guideline 2026
targetedMedications.memoryUse: tPA thrombolytic used to dissolve pathologic clots in selected emergency indications.
targetedMedications.memoryDanger: Major danger = serious bleeding/ICH. In stroke, hemorrhage must be excluded before treatment and BP must be controlled.
targetedMedications.mechanism: Recombinant tissue plasminogen activator that activates fibrin-bound plasminogen to plasmin, producing fibrinolysis.
targetedMedications.mechanismBasis: Drug-specific administration and safety were checked against current DailyMed Activase prescribing information. Stroke timing and BP context were aligned with the 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline. The U.S. product label still states a 3-hour stroke window, while the newer guideline supports eligible patients within 4.5 hours; follow the newest applicable local stroke protocol.

targetedFaqs.question: AF vs SVT: how are they different, can they come from the same place, and why can one patient have both?

sections.label: Core distinction
sections.text: Both are supraventricular arrhythmias, but they usually do not arise from the same mechanism. AF is disorganized atrial activation. In bedside shorthand, 'SVT' usually means a regular narrow-complex re-entrant tachycardia such as AVNRT or AVRT, although technically several atrial rhythms are supraventricular.

sections.label: What the ECG usually looks like
sections.text: AF is typically irregularly irregular with no consistent P waves. Typical AVNRT/orthodromic AVRT is usually very regular and narrow-complex; P waves may be hidden in or just after the QRS. Atrial flutter with fixed conduction can also look like a regular SVT.

sections.label: Do they come from the same place?
sections.text: Usually no. AF commonly involves atrial triggers and substrate, often around the pulmonary veins/left atrium. AVNRT uses a re-entry circuit in or near the AV node. AVRT uses the AV node plus an accessory pathway. Atrial tachycardia is another SVT and can arise from an atrial focus, so its anatomical origin may be closer to an AF trigger region.

sections.label: Why can one patient have both?
sections.text: Different arrhythmia mechanisms can coexist in the same patient. Shared problems such as structural heart disease, ischemia, heart failure, atrial enlargement, hypoxia, electrolyte disturbance, infection/fever, thyroid disease or stimulants can increase atrial electrical instability. A rapid re-entrant SVT can also sometimes trigger AF. Current AF guidance recognizes an important association between early-onset AF and re-entrant supraventricular tachyarrhythmias.

sections.label: Nursing bedside approach
sections.text: Do not treat the monitor label alone. Assess the patient first, check pulse/BP/SpO₂, inspect the rhythm strip and obtain a 12-lead ECG when available. In a tachyarrhythmia with hypotension, acute altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort or acute heart failure, escalate immediately; current AHA guidance directs synchronized cardioversion for persistent unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse.

sections.label: Important danger: AF with pre-excitation/WPW
sections.text: Pre-excited AF may be very fast and irregular, often with a wide or changing QRS, and can deteriorate to ventricular fibrillation. AV-nodal blocking drugs can be harmful in pre-excited AF because they may favor conduction through the accessory pathway. Treat this as an urgent expert/advanced-life-support problem rather than as ordinary regular SVT.

sections.label: Memory
sections.text: AF = usually irregularly irregular atrial chaos. Typical AVNRT/AVRT = usually regular narrow-complex re-entry. Same patient can have both; always identify the actual rhythm and patient stability before acting.
